problem:
A hospital plans the night shift for two wards.

1. First, before anyone knows how the night will go, the ward manager may book overtime:
   up to two shifts for ward A and up to two for ward B, each costing 6. One booked shift
   covers 4 patients on the ward it was booked for.
2. Then one of the two wards receives an unplanned admission wave. Exactly one ward is
   affected, and the manager has no influence over which. The affected ward has to cover
   4 additional patients.
3. Only afterwards may the manager call in agency staff. Two agency nurses are available
   at 3 each, and each covers 4 patients on whichever ward they are sent to. At most one
   agency nurse can be reached at that hour.

Ward A must cover 4 patients before any wave, ward B must cover 8. Every booking is a
yes/no decision on a single shift. Minimise the total cost for the worst case.
reference_qlp:
MINIMIZE
6 a1 + 6 a2 + 6 b1 + 6 b2 + 3 g1 + 3 g2
SUBJECT TO
E_ward_a: 4 a1 + 4 a2 + 4 g1 - 4 w1 >= 4
E_ward_b: 4 b1 + 4 b2 + 4 g2 - 4 w2 >= 8
E_agency: 1 g1 + 1 g2 <= 1
U_one_wave: 1 w1 + 1 w2 = 1
BOUNDS
0 <= a1 <= 1
0 <= a2 <= 1
0 <= b1 <= 1
0 <= b2 <= 1
0 <= w1 <= 1
0 <= w2 <= 1
0 <= g1 <= 1
0 <= g2 <= 1
BINARIES
a1 a2 b1 b2 w1 w2 g1 g2
EXISTS
a1 a2 b1 b2 g1 g2
ALL
w1 w2

a2
b1

w1
w2
g1
g2
END

problem:
Three regions of a data centre network each need guaranteed throughput, and
one of the three uplinks will fail tonight. Which one is unknown and must be assumed to be
the worst case; exactly one fails, never two, never none.

Capacity is bought in two rounds. In the first round, before the failure, the operator may
lease up to two dedicated lines per region at 7 each; a dedicated line carries 5 units of
throughput for its own region and for no other. A failed uplink costs the affected region
5 units of throughput.

In the second round, once the failure is visible, the operator may activate emergency
bandwidth at 3 per block, again 5 units for one region. Emergency bandwidth is cheap
because it is scarce: only two blocks exist in total, to be distributed across all regions
as the operator sees fit.

Guaranteed throughput is 5 units for the first region, 10 for the second, 5 for the third.
Leases and blocks are taken as whole units or not at all. Minimise the worst-case cost.

One of the two locations will then be closed by the authorities for part of the shoot —

Afterwards, with the closure known, the producer may rent up to two replacement packages

A supplier serves 3 products and decides in three steps.

Step 1: buy advance units. Up to 3 may be bought for each product, at a cost of 5 per unit. An advance unit bought for a product provides 4 units of capacity for that product only.

Step 2: a disruption hits, outside the supplier's control. Exactly one of the 3 products is affected — never none, never more than one — and its demand rises by 4. Which product it is must be assumed to be the worst possible choice.

Step 3: after seeing which product was hit, buy express units. Up to 1 may be bought for each product, at 3 per unit, and each also provides 4 units of capacity for its product. Express units are cheaper than advance units, but at most 2 of them may be bought in total across all products.

Baseline demand is 2 for product 1, 3 for product 2, 8 for product 3. For every product, the capacity bought for it must cover its baseline demand plus the increase if it is the product that was hit. Every purchase is a yes/no decision on a single unit. Minimise the total cost in the worst case.

problem:

The decisions happen strictly in this order:
1. Decide how many of two regular runs to start in period 1, each costing 3.
2. A demand shock for period 1 either happens or not, outside the plant's control; if it happens it adds 1 to period-1 demand.
3. Knowing whether that shock happened, decide how many of two regular runs to start in period 2, each costing 2.
4. A second demand shock either happens or not, again outside the plant's control; if it happens it adds 1 to period-2 demand.
5. Finally, knowing both shocks, start up to two emergency runs at 6 each.

Period-1 demand is 5 plus the first shock, and must be met by period-1 production alone. Cumulative demand over both periods is 16 plus both shocks, and must be met by everything produced.

Each run is a yes/no decision. The plan must work for every combination of shocks. Minimise the total cost in the worst case.
